\chapter{Four Core Colours}
\label{ch:hi-core-colours}
\hlchaptermodality{11}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name black, white, red and blue in Hindi and say which of them came from Sanskrit and which from Persian.}

Say \hi{लाल} and \hi{नीला} beside \hi{काला} and \hi{सफ़ेद}, keeping nīla and 'indigo' honestly linked by trade rather than by sound.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\hi{काला} \hi{सफ़ेद}]{\hi{काला}, \hi{सफ़ेद} (kālā, safed) — black and white}

\label{lesson:HI-C11-kaalaa-safed}



\begin{quote}
Hindi's word for black hides something bigger inside it: the very same word Sanskrit uses for \textbf{time itself} — and for death.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{काला} — black, time, and death, tangled together}
\textbf{\hi{काला}} (\emph{kālā}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{black},\textquotedblright{} from Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{काल}} (\emph{kāla}), a word that covers both \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{black/dark}\textquotedblright{} \textbf{and} \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{time}.\textquotedblright{} Sanskrit's own tradition ties the two together poetically — \textbf{time devours everything}, and that devouring is imagined as \emph{dark} — and the same word names the fierce goddess \textbf{Kālī} (\textquotedblleft{}the black/dark one\textquotedblright{}) and stands as an epithet of \textbf{Yama}, the god of death. Be honest, though: whether \textquotedblleft{}black\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{} are truly \textbf{one and the same root}, or two separate ancient words that Sanskrit poetry and theology later \textbf{fused} into a single idea, is a real, still-debated question among linguists — the cultural connection is certain; the precise etymology underneath it is not.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{सफ़ेद} — a Persian loan}
\textbf{\hi{सफ़ेद}} (\emph{safed}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{white}\textquotedblright{} — borrowed from \textbf{Persian} (\ar{سفید} \emph{safēd}), the same kind of Persian-into-Hindi borrowing you've already met in \textbf{\hi{माफ़}} (\emph{māf}, \textquotedblleft{}forgiven,\textquotedblright{} from the \textquotedblleft{}sorry\textquotedblright{} lesson). Notice the \textbf{\hi{नुक़्ता}} (\emph{nuqtā}, the dot under \hi{फ}): it turns \emph{pha} into \textbf{fa}, the tell-tale mark of a sound that arrived from Persian or Arabic.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kāla\textquotedblright{} — time/black/death, then \textquotedblleft{}kālā\textquotedblright{} — black
  \item \textquotedblleft{}safed\textquotedblright{} — white, a Persian loan
  \item the dot — \hi{नुक़्ता} under \hi{फ} turns pha into fa
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\hi{काला}}'s root \textbf{\hi{काल}} (\emph{kāla}) also mean, besides \textquotedblleft{}black\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Time\textquotedblright{}} — and by extension, \textbf{death}; the same word names the goddess \textbf{Kālī} and Yama's epithet \textbf{Kāla}.) Is it settled that \textquotedblleft{}black\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{} are the same root? (\textbf{No} — the cultural link is real and ancient, but linguists still debate whether it's one true root or two words later fused.) Where does \textbf{\hi{सफ़ेद}} come from? (\textbf{Persian} \emph{safēd} — the same kind of loan as \emph{māf}, \textquotedblleft{}sorry.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\hi{लाल} \hi{नीला}]{\hi{लाल}, \hi{नीला} (lāl, nīlā) — a gemstone's name, and India's dye}

\label{lesson:HI-C11-laal-niila}



\begin{quote}
One more color pair, and one more Persian loan — plus a Sanskrit word connected to why English itself says \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{indigo}.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{लाल} — named for a gem, not a color}
\textbf{\hi{लाल}} (\emph{lāl}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{red}\textquotedblright{} — borrowed from Persian \textbf{\ar{لعل}} (properly \emph{laʿl}, with a middle \emph{ʿayn} the Hindi/Persian pronunciation \emph{lāl} smooths over), which originally named a specific \textbf{deep-red gemstone} (a ruby or spinel), and only later widened to mean the color itself. Hindi's everyday word for \textquotedblleft{}red\textquotedblright{} started life as a jeweler's word.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{नीला} — Sanskrit's dark blue, and the world's word for indigo}
\textbf{\hi{नीला}} (\emph{nīlā}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{blue},\textquotedblright{} from Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{नील}} (\emph{nīla}), \textquotedblleft{}dark blue\textquotedblright{} — also the name of the \textbf{indigo plant} and its dye. Here's the honest, careful version of a famous connection: English \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}indigo\textquotedblright{}} does \textbf{not} come from \emph{nīla} by sound change. It comes from \textbf{Greek} \emph{indikón}, simply meaning \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the Indian {[}thing{]}}\textquotedblright{} — because Greek and Roman traders imported the blue dye \textbf{from India}. So \emph{nīlā} and \textquotedblleft{}indigo\textquotedblright{} aren't the same word evolving — they're two \textbf{separate} words for the same dye, one Indian (\emph{nīla}, describing the color) and one foreign (\emph{indikón}, describing the dye's \emph{origin}). The connection is real, but it's a connection of \textbf{history and trade}, not of sound.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}lāl\textquotedblright{} — red, originally a gemstone's name
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nīlā\textquotedblright{} — blue, from Sanskrit nīla
  \item the honest distinction — nīla and \textquotedblleft{}indigo\textquotedblright{} are two different words linked by trade, not by sound
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \textbf{\hi{लाल}} originally name, before it meant \textquotedblleft{}red\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{A deep red gemstone}, borrowed from Persian.) Does English \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{indigo}\textquotedblright{} come directly from Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{नील}} \emph{nīla}? (\textbf{No} — indigo is from Greek \emph{indikón}, \textquotedblleft{}the Indian {[}thing{]},\textquotedblright{} describing where the dye came from; \emph{nīla} and \textquotedblleft{}indigo\textquotedblright{} are two separate words connected by history, not by sound change.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ā]{\hi{◌ा} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:HI-S06-vowel-sign-aa}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \hi{◌्} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \hi{◌ा}}
\textbf{\hi{◌ा}} — \emph{ā}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and \textbf{replaces} the \emph{a} built into it with \emph{ā}. Replaces, not adds — the \emph{a} is gone.

Where it sits: a vertical bar to the right of the consonant.

Worked through: \textbf{\hi{न}} + \textbf{\hi{◌ा}} = \textbf{\hi{ना}} — \emph{nā}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \hi{◌ा} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{शिरोरेखा}} \emph{shirorekhā} — the head-line that Devanagari letters hang from
  \item \textbf{\hi{मेरा}} \emph{merā} — my
  \item \textbf{\hi{क्या}} \emph{kyā} — what
  \item \textbf{\hi{मेरा} \hi{नाम}} \emph{merā nām} — assemble my name from known letters and show word spacing as two head-lines
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \hi{◌ा} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \hi{◌ा} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \hi{◌ा} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\hi{शिरोरेखा}  ·  \hi{मेरा}  ·  \hi{नमस्ते}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \hi{◌ा} three times, saying \emph{ā} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \hi{◌ा} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \hi{◌ा}? What vowel does it put on the consonant it attaches to — and what does it take off? (\textbf{Puts \emph{ā} on; takes the built-in \emph{a} off.}) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ya]{\hi{य} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:HI-S115-letter-ya}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \hi{ह} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \hi{य}}
\textbf{\hi{य}} — \emph{ya}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{y}, it is \textbf{ya}.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a clockwise inner curl
  \item a lower bowl rising to the right-stem junction
  \item a top-to-bottom right stem
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

You already say these, and every one of them has \hi{य} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{धन्यवाद}} — thank you (dhanyavād — formal, Sanskritic)
  \item \textbf{\hi{शुक्रिया}} — thanks (shukriyā — everyday, Persian/Arabic-derived)
  \item \textbf{\hi{क्या}} \emph{kyā} — what
  \item \textbf{\hi{कृपया}} \emph{kṛpayā} — please (kṛpayā — \textquotedblleft{}kindly,\textquotedblright{} from kṛpā \textquotedblleft{}grace/compassion\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \hi{य}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start beneath the headline, curve clockwise around the inner curl, and finish at the left waist
  \item \textbf{2.} lift at that waist, curve down and right around the lower bowl, and rise to the right-stem junction
  \item \textbf{3.} lift and draw the right stem top-to-bottom
  \item \textbf{4.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 3.} The pen comes up 3 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
Verified four-stroke teaching form; another animated learner source joins the inner curl and lower bowl.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Opiaterein, ‘Deva-\hi{य}-order.gif’, strokes 1–4, Wikimedia Commons, 10 May 2009.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \hi{य} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\hi{धन्यवाद}  ·  \hi{शुक्रिया}  ·  \hi{नमस्ते}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \hi{य} three times, saying \emph{ya} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \hi{य} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \hi{य}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ya}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
